Alphabet soup of the economy? My take on C vs K, and  
@michaelrstrain.bsky.social makes great points, too. www.npr.org/2026/08/13/n...
Adding my pre-CPI thread here, which talks about the FOMC reaction function from the June minutes. Today's CPI cleared the bar for a good CPI. bsky.app/profile/clau...

Implications for the Fed: good news. Disinflation, even as the Fed's been on hold so far this year, supports its stance. It's too soon to say whether a hold will be appropriate in September—more data coming—but the chances of a hike edged down some today.

The breadth of inflation narrowed in July, reducing one of the risks the Fed is monitoring. The share of the CPI basket with prices rising 5%+ fell in July and is back to the average levels in 1997-2005, when inflation was close to 2%. This may be the best news in today's report!

There were good details, particularly non-housing core services aka supercore. That's been sticky inflation in recent years and picked up earlier this year. June saw a decline, owing to some outliers. Supercore rose 0.2% in July, which is well below the pace early in the year.

The July CPI continued to build the case for disinflation. Core CPI rose 0.2% in July (or annualized 2.6%), firmer than flat prices in June, but still helping to move the trend down. Even so, two months is not enough, and the PPI will also shape whether it's a good PCE print.
The world’s big central banks are rethinking how they communicate with the public, threatening a transparency revolution that made policymakers more accountable and tamped down market volatility

I agree with Guy’s skepticism. AND as a former Board economist who worked on one of the Fed‘s early projects with alternative data in **2016** I can affirm many Fed economists have been working on such data for a decade.

Does the July CPI need to be as soft as the June CPI? No, but it needs to fit the bill of a good CPI. The consensus for core CPI of 0.2% would probably count, though lower is better.

Then the PPI needs to behave too. It's PCE that needs to show disinflation, or a hike is likely.

media-press.quote: So what’s a better place for info? I used to point students to #EconTwitter, but the algo there is awful, amplifying pile-ons over convos, and Elon drove many off the platform. Bluesky doesn't quite feel like it has critical mass yet, but it might be closer.

Economics Job Market Rumors started back when I was on the job market 20 years ago. I remember how much the uncertainty of getting a job makes you seek out any kind of info. But quality matters. An anon forum was never going to cut it. And it would breed bad behavior. It did.

I heard this week that the cesspool econ website EJMR went dark. it’s been offline for over a week now. no tears shed here. solid poetic justice that unrelenting AI bot attacks appear to have been its downfall. but it raises a question: where does the demand for info go next?
